strengths: The problem is well motivated: predicting behavior under changing external feedback is relevant to cognitive modeling and adaptive interventions. Integrating task representations, evidence accumulation, and reinforcement learning offers a plausible structured approach.

The two-day study provides substantial repeated behavioral measurements across four feedback conditions, with 36 participants retained for analysis. Evaluation includes personalized models and leave-one-participant-out testing, which usefully examines transfer to unseen participants.

The empirical results show promise. Learned task features outperform the tested raw-input representations, and hybrid DRL achieves lower aggregate MAPE than pure DRL in all four evaluation settings. The reported convergence time also improves substantially, from 38.30 to 4.42 minutes.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are unavailable in the supplied PDF. Appendices S2–S6 are repeatedly referenced but absent, leaving the adaptive feedback rule, DDM update equations and parameter construction, RL algorithm and reward, and important training settings insufficiently specified. These omissions prevent confident assessment and reproduction of the central method.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the cognitive model. Pure DRL removes both the DDM and frame-by-frame processing, so the comparison changes multiple factors simultaneously. A matched sequential neural predictor, a direct supervised response-time regressor using the same information, and a fitted DDM with stimulus-dependent parameters would provide stronger evidence. The distinction from existing cognitive-model/neural-network combinations and RL–DDM work also needs sharper articulation.

The predictive improvements are modest and lack uncertainty estimates sufficient to establish robustness. Figure 3(m) reports general-level MAPE of 0.2999 versus 0.3034 and LOPO MAPE of 0.2905 versus 0.3037. Participant-level paired confidence intervals and variability across training runs are needed. It is also unclear whether normalization, SVM fitting, and hyperparameter selection are confined to each training fold; the LOPO description alone does not establish that the complete pipeline excludes held-out participants.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Matching final response times does not identify the intermediate evidence-accumulation trajectory: many action sequences can produce the same stopping time. Figure 3 even shows nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories in the no-pressure condition, suggesting that the agent can also correct baseline prediction errors. Stimulus ablations, controlled changes to temporal feedback, or independent process measurements are needed to distinguish predictive adjustment from an explanation of human cognition.

The behavioral conclusions require greater qualification. Only seven analyzed participants remain in the random-feedback group, and the criteria for excluding three 'extreme outliers' are unspecified. The reported significant pairwise response-time difference is between random and no feedback; this does not establish superiority over every alternative. Sensitivity analyses and clearer accounting of which participants and trials constitute the approximately 25,000-sample modeling dataset would strengthen the conclusions.

Minor reporting issues should be corrected. The counts in Figure 2(g) imply approximately 99.61% accuracy, rather than the stated 99.93%. The densely packed figures also make numerical comparisons difficult; a compact results table would improve auditability.
